claims.text: An algorithm is a solution to a problem expressed as a sequence of defined steps: each step is unambiguous, and the steps in order take the input to the result.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An algorithm works because its steps are defined, ordered and complete, so the same input passes through the same steps to the same result, and the solution can be followed without its designer present.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A suitable identifier name states what the data it holds represents, so TotalPrice reads as a total and not a count, and the algorithm can be checked against the problem it solves.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Data used by a problem is represented by named constants and variables: a constant holds a value fixed for the whole run, and a variable holds a value that changes as the steps proceed.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An algorithm takes input, processes it and produces output, and a pseudocode program shows the three: INPUT statements bring values in, the process steps work on them, and OUTPUT statements present the result.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The three basic constructs are sequence, selection and iteration: sequence runs steps in order, selection chooses between paths with IF or CASE, and iteration repeats steps with FOR, WHILE or REPEAT.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A count-controlled loop (FOR ... TO ... NEXT) runs a known number of times, whereas a conditional loop (WHILE ... ENDWHILE or REPEAT ... UNTIL) runs until its condition changes.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: An algorithm can be documented in three ways - structured English, a flowchart, or pseudocode - and the three show the same steps in different languages, so each can be turned into either of the others.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A flowchart documents an algorithm as boxes and arrows: start and end in rounded shapes, process steps in rectangles, input and output in parallelograms, and decisions in diamonds with a labelled Yes exit and a labelled No exit.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Writing pseudocode from a structured English description works statement by statement, with the description's conditions becoming IF conditions or loop conditions, and its sentences becoming one or more pseudocode statements.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Drawing a flowchart from pseudocode works construct by construct: each sequence step becomes a rectangle, each selection a diamond with two labelled exits, and each iteration a loop back to its condition.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Stepwise refinement starts with the problem as one statement, then breaks each statement into more detailed statements, step by step, until each statement is at the level of detail needed to write pseudocode.

verification.method: Authored originally for 9618 AS under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Logic statements define parts of an algorithm solution with AND, OR and NOT, so the conditions of selections and loops are built from them and say exactly when each part acts.
